patient.chief_complaint: Bilateral eyelid drooping of decades duration initially diagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia — now worsening with new fatigability
patient.hpi:
A 53-year-old Ghanaian woman with hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus presented to the neurology clinic for evaluation of worsening bilateral eyelid ptosis and increasing generalized fatigue. She first noticed left upper eyelid drooping at approximately age 20, which gradually worsened over years and was eventually followed by bilateral ptosis. She reported no diplopia, diurnal variation, dysphagia, or other muscle weakness throughout this time. She had multiple prior evaluations, and the consistent clinical picture — gradual onset without fatigability, no diplopia, absent ice pack test response at initial evaluation — led to a clinical diagnosis of chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO).

Over the past 8 months, however, she noticed new and different symptoms: significant fatigue with prolonged talking or chewing, muffled voice quality that was worse in the afternoon, and difficulty completing her usual 30-minute walk due to bilateral leg fatigue. She also experienced occasional choking with liquids. Crucially, she noted for the first time that the eyelid drooping seemed more pronounced when tired and somewhat better in the morning — a pattern she had not observed before. She also reported a sensation of double images on lateral gaze, which resolved with eye closure.

Her ocular history included bilateral elevated intraocular pressures (managed with timolol eye drops) and bilateral cataract surgery 3 years prior (significant improvement in acuity post-operatively). She had no family history of neuromuscular or mitochondrial disease. On examination, complete bilateral ptosis was present. The ice pack test produced a 4 mm improvement bilaterally, which was POSITIVE — in contrast to prior documented negative result. Restricted extraocular movements were present, more pronounced in vertical gaze. A new finding was fatigable palate elevation on the SLURP test, absent in prior evaluations.

physical_exam.general: Well-appearing middle-aged woman; alert and cooperative; bilateral ptosis visible immediately
physical_exam.neurological: Complete bilateral ptosis (left > right). Positive ice pack test (4 mm improvement bilaterally in 5 minutes). Extraocular movements restricted in all directions, more so in vertical gaze; no ophthalmoplegia pain. Diplopia elicitable on extreme lateral gaze but not in primary position. Fatigable palate elevation on SLURP test (new finding). No tongue fasciculations. Limb strength: hip flexors 4/5 bilaterally (fatigable), otherwise 5/5. Deep tendon reflexes 2+ symmetric. Cerebellar examination normal. Sensation intact throughout. Gait normal.
physical_exam.cardiovascular: Regular rate and rhythm; no murmurs
physical_exam.abdomen: Soft; mild central adiposity; no organomegaly
physical_exam.extremities: No edema; bilateral posterior subcapsular lens opacity noted by patient (post-cataract surgery)

ground_truth.primary_diagnosis: AChR antibody–positive generalized myasthenia gravis, evolving from decades-long ocular presentation misdiagnosed as CPEO (G70.01)

differential.key_features: Prior diagnosis; however, positive ice pack test, new fatigability, diurnal variation, and positive AChR antibodies definitively exclude CPEO
No pigmentary retinopathy, no cardiac conduction defect, no cerebellar ataxia — cannot diagnose KSS; criteria not met
Myotonic dystrophy can cause ptosis but also causes myotonia, grip release difficulty, cataracts, frontal balding; no these features; normal CK
Normal TSH; ptosis (not lid retraction); no proptosis; normal orbital MRI extraocular muscles

optimal_actions.action: Reassess ice pack test — positive result changes prior CPEO diagnosis
MG antibody panel (AChR binding, blocking, modulating, anti-MuSK)
SFEMG and RNS to confirm NMJ dysfunction
Recognize timolol eye drops as MG exacerbant and discontinue — switch to latanoprost or dorzolamide
Initiate pyridostigmine; add prednisone and azathioprine for generalized MG management

critical_actions: Recognize that positive ice pack test invalidates prior CPEO diagnosis — it is >97% specific for MG
Order AChR antibody panel as definitive serological diagnosis
Identify and discontinue timolol eye drops — beta-blockers exacerbate MG
Screen for thymoma with CT chest despite age >50 (thymus involuted but still relevant)
Assess for fatigable limb weakness — confirms generalized rather than ocular-only disease
Mitochondrial workup deferred given positive serology — AChR antibody is diagnostic
contraindicated_actions: Do not continue timolol eye drops — contraindicated in MG
Do not prescribe beta-blockers in any form without considering MG risk
Do not pursue muscle biopsy for mitochondrial disease before ordering AChR antibody (unnecessary if AChR positive)
Do not diagnose CPEO in a patient with positive ice pack test and AChR antibodies
key_reasoning_points: The diagnostic puzzle: decades-long 'CPEO' diagnosis was incorrect; the key change is a NOW-positive ice pack test and new fatigability, which should trigger AChR antibody testing
CPEO and MG can share features (bilateral ptosis, ophthalmoplegia) but are distinguished by fatigability, diurnal variation, ice pack test, and AChR antibody
Timolol eye drops are a critical hidden drug-disease interaction that may have been worsening MG for years — beta-blockers impair NMJ transmission
KSS criteria not met: no pigmentary retinopathy, no cardiac conduction defect, no cerebellar ataxia
Positive AChR antibody is the single most valuable test: >99% specific for MG if markedly elevated; precludes need for muscle biopsy
Late-onset MG can first present with pure ocular features before evolving to generalized disease years later

red_herrings.data_point: Prior CPEO diagnosis over 30 years — anchoring bias
red_herrings.intended_effect: Long-standing prior diagnosis creates anchoring bias toward continuing the CPEO label despite new clinical features
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Positive ice pack test + new fatigability + AChR antibody = MG; prior CPEO diagnosis was incorrect

red_herrings.data_point: Borderline lactate/pyruvate ratio suggesting possible mitochondrial disease
red_herrings.intended_effect: Borderline L/P ratio with CPEO history increases suspicion for mitochondrial myopathy
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Serum lactate is normal; borderline L/P ratio is non-specific; definitive AChR antibody supersedes mitochondrial concern

metadata.condition_name: Myasthenia gravis misdiagnosed as chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia
metadata.difficulty_description: Diagnostic puzzle: prior CPEO diagnosis creates anchoring bias; new fatigability and positive ice pack test are the pivotal clues; timolol eye drops as hidden contributing drug-disease interaction

output.interpretation: AChR binding antibody markedly elevated at 5.8 nmol/L (reference < 0.4 nmol/L). AChR blocking antibody positive. Anti-MuSK antibody negative. Anti-acetylcholine receptor antibodies are found in a subset of patients with neuromuscular junction disorders; an elevated result supports but is not exclusive to myasthenia gravis. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description:
SINGLE-FIBER EMG — ORBICULARIS OCULI

Indication: Evaluation of bilateral ptosis

RESULTS:
  MCD: 58 µs [normal <35 µs] MARKEDLY ABNORMAL
  Blocking: 18% of potential pairs
  Fiber density: 2.1 (mildly elevated, borderline)

IMPRESSION: Markedly increased mean consecutive difference with 18% blocking, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Mildly elevated fiber density is a borderline finding. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: SFEMG (orbicularis oculi): MCD 58 µs with 18% blocking — markedly increased jitter consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

findings.description:
REPETITIVE NERVE STIMULATION STUDY

Indication: Neuromuscular junction evaluation

TECHNIQUE: 3 Hz RNS, orbicularis oculi, nasalis, deltoid

RESULTS:
  Orbicularis oculi: Decrement 16% [>10% abnormal] ABNORMAL
  Nasalis: Decrement 13% ABNORMAL
  Deltoid (proximal): Decrement 11% ABNORMAL

IMPRESSION: Abnormal decremental response at 3 Hz in cranial and proximal limb muscles, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

output.impression: RNS: 16% decrement orbicularis, 13% nasalis, 11% deltoid — decremental responses in cranial and proximal muscles, consistent with a disorder of neuromuscular transmission. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.title: Clinical literature
results.content:
LITERATURE SEARCH: CPEO vs Ocular MG — Diagnostic Pitfalls

KEY FINDINGS:
1. ICE PACK TEST: Sensitivity 80%, specificity 97% for MG ptosis when positive. Can be negative early in MG.
2. CPEO FEATURES: Symmetric, slowly progressive, no diurnal variation, negative ice pack test, elevated CK or abnormal muscle biopsy in some, maternal inheritance pattern, associated pigmentary retinopathy in KSS.
3. MG FEATURES: Positive ice pack test, fatigability, diurnal variation (worse in afternoon), AChR antibodies, abnormal RNS/SFEMG.
4. DIAGNOSTIC OVERLAP: MG can be initially mischaracterized as CPEO when early features are atypical; fatigability may develop years later as disease evolves.
5. TIMOLOL AND NEUROMUSCULAR TRANSMISSION: Beta-blockers, including topical ophthalmic timolol, have been reported to interfere with neuromuscular transmission in patients with disorders of the NMJ; prostaglandin analogs or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are alternatives without known NMJ effects.

output.summary: CPEO vs MG: ice pack test, fatigability, and AChR antibody are key distinguishing features; beta-blocker topical agents reported to affect NMJ transmission.

interactions:
DRUG INTERACTION REVIEW — TIMOLOL (OPHTHALMIC) AND NEUROMUSCULAR JUNCTION DISORDERS

Query: Beta-blocker timolol (ophthalmic) in patients with disorders of neuromuscular transmission

FINDINGS:
  TIMOLOL (topical beta-blocker):
  - Systemic absorption occurs with topical ophthalmic administration (~60-70% via nasolacrimal duct)
  - Beta-blockers have been reported to impair neuromuscular transmission in susceptible patients
  - Multiple case reports describe worsening of neuromuscular junction disease with topical beta-blocker use
  - Beta-blockers are generally used with caution in conditions affecting NMJ function
  - Effect is dose-dependent; 0.5% timolol BID achieves measurable systemic levels

  ALTERNATIVES WITHOUT REPORTED NMJ EFFECTS:
  - Prostaglandin analogs (e.g., latanoprost 0.005% once daily)
  - Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors (e.g., dorzolamide 2% BID)
warnings: Timolol (ophthalmic): systemic absorption reported; beta-blockers associated with NMJ transmission impairment in susceptible patients; prostaglandin analogs and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors are alternatives.
